source_text: Duae sunt uiae per quas humanam uitam progredi necesse est, una quae in caelum ferat, altera quae ad inferos deprimat: quas et poetae in carminibus et philosophi in disputationibus suis induxerunt. et quidem philosophi alteram uirtutum esse noluerunt, alteram uitiorum, eamque quae sit assignata uirtutibus; primo aditu esse arduam et confragosam: in qua si quis difficultate superata in summum eius euaserit, habere eum de cetero planum iter, lucidum amoenumque campum et omnium laborum suorum capere fructus uberes atque iucundos; quos autem primi aditus difficultas deterruerit, eos in illam uitiorum uiam labi atque deflectere, quae primo ingressu sit quasi amoena multoque tritior, deinde cum in ea paulo ulterius processerint, amoenitatis illius speciem repente subduci, exoriri autem uiam praecipitem, nunc saxis asperam nunc obductam sentibus nunc gurgitibus intercisam uel torrentibus rapidam, ut laborare haerere labi cadere sit necesse. quae omnia eo proferuntur, ut appareat in uirtutibus capiendis labores esse maximos, in perceptis autem maximos fructus et solidas atque incorruptas uoluptates, uitia uero quibusdam delenimentis naturalibus inlicere animos hominum et inanium iucunditatum specie captos ad acerbas amaritudines miseriasque perducere. sapiens prorsus disputatio, si uirtutum ipsarum formas ac terminos scirent. non enim didicerant uel quae sint uel quid eas mercedis a deo maneat: quod nos his duobus libris docebimus. hi uero quia ignorabant aut dubitabant animas hominum inmortales esse, et uirtutes et uitia terrenis honoribus aut poenis aestimauerunt. omnis ergo haec de duabus uiis disputatio ad frugalitatem ac luxuriam spectat. dicunt enim humanae uitae cursum Y litterae similem, quod unus quisque hominum cum primae adulescentiae limen adtigerit et in eum locum uenerit, partis ubi se uia findit in ambas, haereat nutabundus ac nesciat in quam se partem potius inclinet; si ducem nactus fuerit qui dirigat ad meliora titubantem, hoc est si aut philosophiam didicerit aut eloquentiam aut aliquid honestae artis quo euadat ad bonam frugem, quod fieri sine labore maximo non potest, honestam et copiosam uitam disputant peracturum; si uero doctorem frugalitatis non muenent, in sinistram uiam quae melioris speciem mentiatur incidere, id est desidiae inertiae luxuriae se tradere, quae suauia quidem uidentur ad tempus uera bona ignoranti, post autem amissa omni dignitate ac re familiari in omnibus miseriis ignominiaque uicturum. ad corpus ergo et ad hanc uitam quam in terra ducimus fines earum uiarum rettulerunt. poetae fortasse melius, qui hoc biuium aput inferos esse uoluerunt, sed in eo falluntur quod eas uias mortuis proposuerunt. utrique ergo uere, sed tamen utrique non recte, quia oportuit uias ipsas ad uitam, fines earum ad mortem referri. nos igitur melius et uerius, qui duas istas uias caeli et inferorum esse dicimus, quia iustis inmortalitas, iniustis poena aeterna proposita est. quomodo autem hae uiae uel in caelum tollant uel ad inferna praecipitent explicabo, aperiamque quae sint uirtutes quas philosophi nescierunt; tum earum quae sint praemia, simul etiam quae sint uitia quaeue eorum supplicia monstrabo. nam fortasse aliquis expectet ut separatim de uitiis ac uirtutibus dicam, cum de bono aut malo disserentibus nobis etiam quod est contrarium possit intellegi. sine enim uirtutes inseras, uitia sua sponte decedent, siue uitia eximas, uirtutes ultro subibunt: sic bonorum ac malorum constituta natura est, ut se inuicem semper obpugnent, semper expellant. ita fit ut neque uitia detrahi sine uirtutibus possint nec uirtutes inseri sine detractione uitiorum. has igitur uias longe aliter inducimus quam induci a philosophis solent, primum quod utrique praepositum esse dicimus ducem utrumque inmortalem, sed alterum honoratum, qui uirtutibus ac bonis praesit, alterum damnatum, qui uitiis ac malis. illi autem m dexteriore tantum uia ducem ponunt neque unum neque perpetuum, siquidem quemlibet doctorem bonae artis inducunt, qui a desidia reuocet homines et frugi esse doceat. sed neque ingredi faciunt in eam uiam nisi pueros et adulescentes, uidelicet quod artes in his discantur aetatibus. nos autem (homines) omnis sexus et generis et aetatis in hoc caeleste iter inducimus, quia deus, qui eius uiae dux est, immortalitatem nulli homini nato negat. forma quoque ipsarum uiarum non ita est ut illi putauerunt. quid enim opus est Y littera in rebus contrariis atque diuersis? sed altera illa melior conuersa est ad solis ortum, altera illa deterior ad occasum, quoniam qui ueritatem ac iustitiam sequitur, is accepto immortalitatis praemio perenni luce potietur, qui autem ab illo malo duce inlectus praetulerit uitia uirtutibus, mendacium ueritati, necesse est ad occasum et tenebras deferatur (aeternas). describam igitur utramque et earum proprietates habitusque monstrabo.
pass_a_gloss: There are two paths by which it is necessary to proceed through human life, one which carries to heaven, the other which presses down to the lower world: which paths both poets in their songs and philosophers in their discussions have introduced. And indeed philosophers have not wanted one path to be of virtues, the other of vices, and they have assigned the one which is to virtues; at the first approach it is steep and rough: in which if someone has overcome the difficulty and has escaped to the top of it, he will have from then on a flat path, a bright and pleasant field, and he will reap the fruits of all his labors, rich and pleasant; but those whom the difficulty of the first approach has deterred, they will slip and turn aside into that path of vices, which at the first entrance is as if pleasant and much more trodden, then when they have proceeded a little further in it, the appearance of that pleasantness is suddenly withdrawn, and a precipitous path arises, now rough with rocks, now obstructed with thorns, now cut off with whirlpools or rapid torrents, so that it is necessary to labor, to stick, to slip, to fall. All these things are brought forth so that it may appear that in taking up virtues there are the greatest labors, but in the virtues that have been taken up there are the greatest fruits and solid and uncorrupted pleasures, and vices indeed allure the minds of men with certain natural enticements and lead those captured by the appearance of empty pleasures to bitter hardships and miseries. This is a wise discussion, if they had known the forms and boundaries of the virtues themselves: for they had not learned what they are or what reward from God remains for them: which we will teach in these two books. But they, because they were ignorant or doubted that the souls of men are immortal, and they estimated virtues and vices by earthly honors or punishments. Therefore, this whole discussion about the two paths looks to frugality and luxury. For they say that the course of human life is similar to the letter Y, because each man, when he has touched the threshold of early youth and has come to that place where the path divides into two, is hesitant and does not know which part he should incline towards; if he has found a leader who directs the stumbling one towards better things, that is, if he has learned philosophy or eloquence or some honorable art by which he may escape to good fruit, which cannot happen without the greatest labor, they discuss that he will lead a honorable and rich life; but if he is not warned by a teacher of frugality, he will fall into the left path, which pretends to be better, that is, he will give himself over to idleness, laziness, luxury, which seem pleasant for a time to one who is ignorant of true goods, but after he has lost all dignity and property, he will live in all miseries and ignominy. Therefore, they have referred the boundaries of those paths to the body and to this life which we lead on earth. Poets perhaps did better, who wanted this fork in the road to be in the lower world, but they are deceived in that they proposed those paths to the dead. Both, therefore, are true, but nevertheless both are not correct, because it was necessary to refer the paths themselves to life, the boundaries of them to death. We, therefore, do better and more truly, who say that those two paths are of heaven and the lower world, because immortality is proposed to the just, eternal punishment to the unjust. But how these paths either raise to heaven or precipitate to the lower world, I will explain and I will reveal what the virtues are which the philosophers did not know; then I will show what are the rewards of those virtues, and at the same time what are the vices and what are their punishments. For perhaps someone expects that I will speak separately about vices and virtues, when we are discussing good or evil, and also what is contrary can be understood. For without virtues, vices will depart of their own accord, or if you remove vices, virtues will come of their own accord: thus the nature of good and evil is established, so that they always fight against each other, always expel each other. It happens, therefore, that vices cannot be removed without virtues, nor can virtues be introduced without the removal of vices. We, therefore, introduce these paths in a much different way than they are usually introduced by philosophers, first because we say that a leader is set over both, each immortal, but one honored, who presides over virtues and goods, the other condemned, who presides over vices and evils. But they place a leader only on the right path, and not one or perpetual, since they introduce any teacher of a good art, who recalls men from laziness and teaches them to be frugal. But they do not make anyone enter into that path except boys and young men, evidently because arts are learned in these ages. We, however, lead all men of every sex and genus and age into this heavenly path, because God, who is the leader of that path, denies immortality to no man born. The form of the paths themselves is also not as they thought. For what need is there of the letter Y in things that are contrary and diverse? But the other, better path is turned towards the rising of the sun, the other, worse path towards the setting, because he who follows truth and justice, having received the reward of immortality, will possess eternal light, but he who, having been allured by that evil leader, has preferred vices to virtues, falsehood to truth, will necessarily be carried away to the setting and darkness (eternal). I will, therefore, describe each path and I will show their properties and habits.

pass_b_english: Two paths lie before us in human life, one that carries us to heaven, another that presses us down to the lower world, and both poets in their songs and philosophers in their treatises have set them forth.

The philosophers, for their part, designated one path for virtue and the other for vice, assigning the steep and rugged first approach to virtue; if someone overcomes that initial difficulty and gains the summit, the way thereafter becomes level, a bright and pleasant field where he reaps rich and delightful fruits from all his labors, but those whom the first steepness deters slip aside into the path of vice, which at its entrance appears pleasant and well‑trodden, yet once they have gone a little farther the pleasantness is suddenly withdrawn and a precipitous way arises, now rough with rocks, now blocked with thorns, now cut off by whirlpools or rapid torrents, so that to toil, to stick, to slip, and to fall becomes inevitable.

All this is set forth to show that the pursuit of virtue entails the greatest labors, but once virtue is attained it yields the greatest fruits and solid, uncorrupted pleasures, while vice allures men's minds with natural enticements and leads those captured by the show of empty pleasures into bitter hardships and miseries.

It would be a wise discussion if the philosophers had known the true forms and boundaries of the virtues themselves, for they had not learned what the virtues are or what reward from God awaits them, and that is what we shall teach in these two books.

Because they were ignorant or doubted that human souls are immortal, they measured virtues and vices by earthly honors or punishments, and so their whole discourse on the two paths looks only to frugality and luxury.

They liken the course of human life to the letter Y: each person, upon reaching the threshold of early youth and arriving at the place where the way divides in two, stands hesitant, not knowing which branch to take; if he finds a guide who directs his stumbling steps toward better things — that is, if he learns philosophy or eloquence or some honorable art by which he may escape to good fruit, which cannot happen without the greatest labor — they say he will lead an honorable and abundant life; but if he lacks a teacher of frugality, he falls into the left‑hand path that pretends to be better, surrendering himself to idleness, inertia, and luxury, which seem sweet for a time to one ignorant of true goods, yet after he has lost all dignity and property he will live in every misery and ignominy.

Thus they referred the boundaries of those paths to the body and to this earthly life; the poets perhaps did better by placing the fork in the lower world, yet they erred in proposing those paths to the dead.
Both, therefore, are true in a sense, yet both are not correct, because the paths themselves ought to be referred to life, their boundaries to death.

We, therefore, speak better and more truly when we say that those two paths are the paths of heaven and the lower world, because immortality is set before the just and eternal punishment before the unjust.

How these paths either raise to heaven or precipitate to the lower world I will explain, and I will reveal the virtues which the philosophers did not know; then I will show the rewards of those virtues, and at the same time the vices and their punishments.

Perhaps someone expects me to treat vices and virtues separately, but when we discuss good or evil the contrary can also be understood: without virtues vices depart of their own accord, or if you remove vices virtues come of their own accord; the nature of good and evil is so constituted that they always fight against each other and always expel each other, so that vices cannot be removed without virtues nor virtues introduced without the removal of vices.

We therefore introduce these paths in a far different way than the philosophers do: first, we say that a leader is set over each, both immortal, but one honored, who presides over virtues and goods, the other condemned, who presides over vices and evils; the philosophers place a leader only on the right‑hand path, and not a single or perpetual one, since they bring in any teacher of a good art who recalls men from laziness and teaches them frugality, and they admit no one to that path except boys and young men, evidently because arts are learned at those ages.
We, however, lead into this heavenly path all people of every sex, kind, and age, because God, who is the leader of that path, denies immortality to no human being born.

The very form of the paths is not as they imagined: what need is there of the letter Y in things that are contrary and diverse? Rather, the better path turns toward the sunrise, the worse toward the sunset, because he who follows truth and justice, having received the reward of immortality, will possess eternal light, while he who, allured by that evil leader, prefers vices to virtues and falsehood to truth, must be carried away to the setting and to darkness eternal.
I will therefore describe each path and show their properties and habits.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text, including the distinction between the philosophers' view (referring paths to the body/earthly life) and Lactantius's view (referring paths to heaven/lower world and boundaries to death). All clauses, including the complex descriptions of the paths and the theological assertions regarding immortality and the nature of virtue/vice, are preserved in both Pass A and Pass B. Scripture citations (none present in this specific excerpt) were not required, but the philosophical and theological distinctions are maintained.

The translation accurately reflects the Latin text, preserving all key concepts, citations, and structure. The title 'Two Paths of Human Life' correctly captures the central theme. No omissions, distortions, or errors in citation are present.
